evidence.note: 'VITE_* variables should not contain sensitive information such as API keys. The values ... are bundled into your source code at build time.'
Next.js 16.3 docs: NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars are exposed to the client; verify auth and authorization inside every Server Action; validate client input; return only what the UI needs, not raw DB records.
Vendor scan of 5,600 vibe-coded apps: 2k+ vulnerabilities, 400+ exposed secrets, many via client bundles (lead only).

ts-secret-in-public-env.whyNotLinter: A regex finds prefixed variables but cannot tell a publishable/anon/DSN key from a secret one (`VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY` has no 'secret' in its name; `VITE_MAPS_API_KEY` is meant to be public). Secret scanners (gitleaks, push protection) match literal key formats, not env references; bundle scanners run after build.
ts-secret-in-public-env.aiRelevance: Agents asked to 'call OpenAI from the app' in a Vite/Next front end reach for `import.meta.env.VITE_…_API_KEY` to make the browser call work; vendor scans of vibe-coded apps report hundreds of secrets exposed in client bundles.
ts-secret-in-public-env.expectedNoise: low — fires only on public-prefixed names; the judgment is whether the named key is a secret, which names like OPENAI_API_KEY/SECRET/SERVICE_ROLE make clear.

evidence.note: CWE-1188 Initialization of a Resource with an Insecure Default.
Fetched: warns against secrets hardcoded in source/config; does NOT explicitly address env fallbacks, so graded C for this rule.

ts-secret-env-fallback.whyNotLinter: `process.env.X || 'literal'` is matchable, but most such fallbacks are fine (PORT, LOG_LEVEL); only the meaning of the variable (secret vs setting) decides it.
ts-secret-env-fallback.aiRelevance: Agents make the app 'run out of the box' by adding `|| 'your-secret-key'` placeholders; these ship to production when the env var is forgotten and make JWTs/sessions forgeable.
ts-secret-env-fallback.expectedNoise: low — the judgment (is this a secret?) is usually obvious from the variable name.
ts-secret-env-fallback.notes: Evidence is one B (CWE) plus a C; below the 2xB bar for built-ins until eval data or findings-log evidence is added.

evidence.note: 'Math.random() does not provide cryptographically secure random numbers. Do not use them for anything related to security.'
CWE-338 Use of Cryptographically Weak PRNG.
Vendor study, 100+ LLMs x 80 tasks: security flaws in 45% of outputs; XSS (CWE-80) 86% failure; SQL injection and weak crypto among tested CWEs.

ts-insecure-random-secret.whyNotLinter: Banning Math.random outright (no-restricted-properties) is noisy because most uses are legitimate; eslint-plugin-security only flags `pseudoRandomBytes`. Whether the value is a token needs the surrounding meaning.
ts-insecure-random-secret.aiRelevance: The `Math.random().toString(36).substring(2)` token idiom is extremely common in training data and agents reuse it for reset codes, invite links and API keys.
ts-insecure-random-secret.expectedNoise: low — purpose is usually named (token, code, secret, invite).

evidence.note: 'Never use a plain == operator. Instead consider ... crypto.timingSafeEqual, which performs a constant time string comparison.'
crypto.timingSafeEqual exists for constant-time comparison (section body not extracted by the fetcher).

ts-secret-compare-not-constant-time.whyNotLinter: eslint-plugin-security `detect-possible-timing-attacks` flags any `===` whose operand name looks secret-ish, which is too noisy for most teams and misses `expected`/`computed` names; knowing which operand is a secret derived from request input needs judgment.
ts-secret-compare-not-constant-time.aiRelevance: Agents writing webhook handlers from memory compute the HMAC correctly and then compare with `===`; GitHub's docs call this out explicitly.
ts-secret-compare-not-constant-time.expectedNoise: low-med — token/role comparisons that are not secrets must be excluded by the `false` list.

evidence.note: jwt.decode: 'This will not verify whether the signature is valid. You should not use this for untrusted messages.'
Next.js 16.3 docs: NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars are exposed to the client; verify auth and authorization inside every Server Action; validate client input; return only what the UI needs, not raw DB records.

ts-jwt-decode-without-verify.whyNotLinter: `jwt.decode` is legitimate in clients and for reading headers before verification; whether the decoded claims feed an authorization decision on the server is semantic.
ts-jwt-decode-without-verify.aiRelevance: When verification fails with a wrong key or algorithm, agents 'fix' auth by switching to decode; middleware that decodes Supabase/Firebase tokens for a user id is a common generated pattern.

evidence.note: Primary defense: parameterized queries.
$queryRawUnsafe/$executeRawUnsafe with interpolated input opens SQL injection; tagged $queryRaw creates prepared statements.
Vendor study, 100+ LLMs x 80 tasks: security flaws in 45% of outputs; XSS (CWE-80) 86% failure; SQL injection and weak crypto among tested CWEs.

ts-sql-interpolated-raw-query.whyNotLinter: Standard ESLint presets have no SQL-injection rule; telling a safe tagged template (`sql`…``) from an unsafe untagged one passed to `$queryRawUnsafe` is the judgment. Semgrep/CodeQL can cover it when they gate CI.
ts-sql-interpolated-raw-query.aiRelevance: Veracode tests SQL injection among its CWEs; agents switch from tagged `$queryRaw` to `$queryRawUnsafe` or string templates to get dynamic ORDER BY/IN lists working.
ts-sql-interpolated-raw-query.notes: Refines generic-menu gen-sql-string-building with TS-specific safe look-alikes. Skip if Semgrep/CodeQL SQLi rules gate CI.

evidence.note: exec/execSync: 'Never pass unsanitized user input to this function. Any input containing shell metacharacters may be used to trigger arbitrary command execution.' Same for spawn/execFile with shell enabled.
Primary defense: avoid the shell; pass command and arguments separately (argument arrays) with allow-list validation.

ts-shell-command-interpolation.whyNotLinter: eslint-plugin-security `detect-child-process` flags every non-literal exec, including safe constant-plus-escaped cases, and is rarely enabled; recognising safe Bun/zx tagged templates versus plain template strings needs judgment.
ts-shell-command-interpolation.aiRelevance: Agents writing CLI tools and build scripts default to `execSync(`…${x}`)` because it is shortest.
ts-shell-command-interpolation.notes: Refines generic-menu gen-shell-command-string with Bun Shell/zx safe look-alikes.

evidence.note: RegExp.escape (Baseline 2025) exists to make user-provided strings safe inside new RegExp(); MDN example of an unescaped '.' matching the wrong domain.
User-controlled patterns enable ReDoS.

ts-regexp-from-input.whyNotLinter: eslint-plugin-security `detect-non-literal-regexp` flags every dynamic RegExp, including ones built from constants or already-escaped values; whether the value is external input and whether it is escaped is the judgment.
ts-regexp-from-input.aiRelevance: Search/filter features generated by agents commonly do `new RegExp(query, 'i')` to get case-insensitive matching.

evidence.note: Redirecting to a request parameter enables phishing; map ids to server-side URLs or validate against an allow-list.
Next.js 16.3 docs: NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars are exposed to the client; verify auth and authorization inside every Server Action; validate client input; return only what the UI needs, not raw DB records.

ts-open-redirect.whyNotLinter: Requires knowing the redirect argument is request input and that no validation happened; CodeQL can track this but standard ESLint presets cannot.
ts-open-redirect.aiRelevance: Login flows generated by agents add `?next=`/`?returnTo=` support and pass it straight to redirect.
ts-open-redirect.notes: Evidence note: next_sec supports input validation generally, not redirects specifically.

evidence.note: 'Arguments to Server Functions are fully client-controlled ... treat them as untrusted input'; 'In any Server Function, make sure to validate that the logged-in user is allowed to perform that action.'
Next.js 16.3 docs: NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars are exposed to the client; verify auth and authorization inside every Server Action; validate client input; return only what the UI needs, not raw DB records.

react-server-action-missing-auth.whyNotLinter: No lint rule knows which calls are mutations or which helpers authenticate; the page-level auth check that agents rely on does not protect the action, and that is a semantic judgment.
react-server-action-missing-auth.aiRelevance: Agents protect the page (redirect if logged out) and assume the action inside is protected; Next.js docs single this out because actions are reachable by direct POST.
react-server-action-missing-auth.expectedNoise: low-med — repos with a DAL doing auth are handled by the 'named data-access function' exception.

evidence.note: 'Arguments to Server Functions are fully client-controlled ... treat them as untrusted input'; 'In any Server Function, make sure to validate that the logged-in user is allowed to perform that action.'
Next.js 16.3 docs: NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars are exposed to the client; verify auth and authorization inside every Server Action; validate client input; return only what the UI needs, not raw DB records.

react-server-action-client-identity.whyNotLinter: Whether an argument named `userId` is the actor or the target resource is a semantic distinction no AST rule can make.
react-server-action-client-identity.aiRelevance: Agents thread `userId` from a client component into the action because the client already has it; this is the classic IDOR the Next.js guide warns about.

'Arguments to Server Functions are fully client-controlled ... treat them as untrusted input'; 'In any Server Function, make sure to validate that the logged-in user is allowed to perform that action.'

react-server-action-returns-record.whyNotLinter: Whether a returned value is a raw row or a trimmed DTO depends on what the called function returns and on field semantics.
react-server-action-returns-record.aiRelevance: Returning the updated record is the shortest way to refresh client state, so agents do it by default; records often include password hashes, emails, internal flags.

evidence.note: Sections 'Notifying parent components about state changes' and 'Passing data to the parent': call onChange in the event handler, not an Effect.
Coverage check: 17 recommended rules incl. set-state-in-effect, purity, refs, immutability, static-components, error-boundaries, exhaustive-deps.

react-effect-notifies-parent.whyNotLinter: react-hooks `set-state-in-effect` targets setState calls; calling a prop callback in an Effect is not flagged by any recommended rule and is legitimate when bridging external events.
react-effect-notifies-parent.aiRelevance: Agents wrapping third-party inputs keep internal state and 'sync' it upward with an Effect, causing double renders and loops when the parent feeds the value back.

evidence.note: Promises passed to use() must be cached; fetch()/uncached async calls/.then() during render create a new Promise every render and keep suspending.

react-use-uncached-promise.whyNotLinter: Whether the argument's Promise is stable across renders depends on what the called function does (cached or not); no react-hooks rule checks it.
react-use-uncached-promise.aiRelevance: `use` is new in React 19 and agents pattern-match it as 'await in a component', writing `use(fetch(url))` directly.
react-use-uncached-promise.expectedNoise: low — `use(getX())` where getX is a cached helper is the main ambiguity; the `false` list says a named cache counts.

evidence.note: dangerouslySetInnerHTML: 'Unless the markup is coming from a completely trusted source, it is trivial to introduce an XSS vulnerability'; 'Only use ... with trusted and sanitized data.'
Lists React dangerouslySetInnerHTML without sanitizing as an XSS sink; recommends DOMPurify.sanitize for user-authored HTML.
Vendor study, 100+ LLMs x 80 tasks: security flaws in 45% of outputs; XSS (CWE-80) 86% failure; SQL injection and weak crypto among tested CWEs.

react-unsanitized-html.whyNotLinter: `react/no-danger` bans the prop outright (opt-in) and cannot tell sanitized or constant HTML from untrusted content.
react-unsanitized-html.aiRelevance: Veracode reports an 86% failure rate on XSS tasks for generated code; agents render markdown/CMS content with `marked()` + dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

evidence.note: Common hydration-mismatch causes: `typeof window !== 'undefined'` checks and browser-only APIs like window.matchMedia in rendering logic.

react-hydration-unsafe-render.whyNotLinter: React Compiler lint rules check purity and refs, not browser-API reads; whether the component is SSR-hydrated is a project fact the rule must infer.
react-hydration-unsafe-render.aiRelevance: Hydration-mismatch errors are among the most common errors agents hit in Next.js, and the usual generated 'fix' is a `typeof window` branch that causes them.
react-hydration-unsafe-render.expectedNoise: med — harmless in pure SPAs; ship disabled by default or gate on Next/Remix detection, or scope with paths such as `app/**`.
react-hydration-unsafe-render.notes: Consider enabling only when the repo has next/remix/react-router framework deps.

evidence.note: Pitfall: 'useFormStatus will not return status information for a <form> rendered in the same component.'

react-useformstatus-same-component.whyNotLinter: Requires relating a hook call to JSX structure and component boundaries; no react-hooks rule covers it.
react-useformstatus-same-component.aiRelevance: New React 19 API; agents trained mostly on pre-19 code call it next to the form like `useState`, producing a button that never shows pending.
react-useformstatus-same-component.notes: Single B source; low frequency but near-zero ambiguity.

evidence.note: Caveat: 'You must wrap any state updates after any async requests in another startTransition to mark them as Transitions.'

react-transition-state-after-await.whyNotLinter: No lint rule models the async-context limitation; it is a documented React caveat about ordering relative to `await`.
react-transition-state-after-await.aiRelevance: Agents adopt async transitions from React 19 examples and set state after the fetch in the same callback.
react-transition-state-after-await.notes: Single B source; React says the limitation will be removed once AsyncContext ships — revisit then.

evidence.note: 'Avoiding recreating the initial state': useState(createInitialTodos()) runs every render; pass the initializer function instead.

react-lazy-initial-state.whyNotLinter: Whether the argument is expensive is a judgment; a rule banning all calls in useState would fire on cheap ones.
react-lazy-initial-state.aiRelevance: Agents persist state with `useState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('x') ?? '[]'))`, re-parsing storage on each render.
react-lazy-initial-state.expectedNoise: low-med — 'expensive' is a judgment; name the storage/parse/build cases literally.
react-lazy-initial-state.notes: Moderate value (performance, not correctness). Overlaps react-hydration-unsafe-render when the initializer reads localStorage in SSR code; both flags are correct.
